title: Combinators: Navigating the DOM Tree 🌳
description: Use descendant, child, adjacent sibling, and general sibling selectors to target elements based on relationships.

slides.title: What Are Combinators? 🔗
slides.content:
# Defining Relationships Between Selectors

Combinators explain how elements are related in the DOM tree. There are four:
- **Descendant combinator** (space): selects elements inside another, at any depth.
- **Child combinator** (`>`): selects direct children only.
- **Adjacent sibling combinator** (`+`): selects the very next sibling.
- **General sibling combinator** (`~`): selects all following siblings.

Understanding these is key to writing efficient, precise CSS.

slides.title: Descendant Combinator (Space) 📦
slides.content:
# Any Level Deep ```css article p { color: #333; } ``` Selects any `

` that is inside an `

`, no matter how many levels deep. Useful for theming sections, but can be over‑broad. Be mindful of performance and side effects.

slides.title: Descendant vs Child

quizData.question: Which combinator selects direct children only?
quizData.explanation: The `>` combinator targets elements that are direct children of the parent.

slides.title: Sibling Combinators 🤝
slides.content:
# Elements Next to Each Other - **Adjacent sibling (`+`):** Targets the first sibling immediately after. ```css h2 + p { font-weight: bold; } ``` Selects the `

` that directly follows an `

` (sharing the same parent). - **General sibling (`~`):** Targets all siblings after (not before). ```css h2 ~ p { color: gray; } ``` Selects every `

` that comes after an `

` under the same parent.

slides.title: Sibling Combinators in Action
slides.content: Styling a headline and the lead paragraph that follows:
slides.codeSnippet:
News

This is the lead.

Another paragraph.

/* Adjacent: only the first p after h2 */ h2 + p { font-size: 1.2em; } /* General: all p after h2 */ h2 ~ p { color: #555; }

quizData.question: `h2 + p` selects all paragraphs that follow an h2, not just the immediate one.
quizData.explanation: `+` selects only the first sibling immediately after. For all following siblings, use `~`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Combine Combinators You can mix them: `article > p + aside` selects an `
` that is the next sibling of a `

` that is a direct child of `

`. Read them right‑to‑left for the target.
